Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Salt Lake City UT
1048 PM MST Fri Nov 13 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Precipitation becomes more widespread overnight with snow levels
  dropping to ~6500 feet behind a cold front that arrives Saturday
  morning, bringing a line of heavier precipitation. 

- Accumulating snow is expected in all mountain areas, especially
  above 8000 feet, and a Winter Weather Advisory is in effect 
  across the southern mountains.

- Two colder storms arrive next week with the potential for some
  valley snowfall.

&&

.DISCUSSION...A negatively-tilted trough is making its way across
the western CONUS this evening. This trough is the result of phasing
between a southern stream system ejecting across the desert 
southwest and a larger system over the PacNW coast. Southerly flow
ahead of the trough axis (which currently extends from the 
Washington coast through western Arizona) remains in place over 
Utah this evening, which has drawn moisture northward into the 
forecast area. Showers have already developed, and will continue 
to increase in coverage overnight. These showers occurring in the 
warm sector will maintain snow levels mainly above 8 kft through 
much of the night.

A cold front is expected to move into western Utah before 12z and
reach the I-15 corridor between 15-17z. Widespread precipitation 
near the cold front is then expected to quickly decrease behind 
it, clearing out in many valleys through the late morning and 
early afternoon timeframe. The exception will be the mountains and
immediate upslope areas where a brief period of favorable 
orographics will maintain precipitation, especially along 
northwest aspects. Additionally, some enhancement off the GSL may 
allow additional showers along the central Wasatch Front and 
adjacent mountains into the afternoon. Snow levels will quickly 
lower with the passage of the cold front, with H7 temperatures 
falling to -4 to -5C towards the end of the precipitation event. 
This would suggest snow levels down to 6.5-7 kft, although the 
greatest (and any real impactful) accumulation can be expected 
above 8-9 kft. Most valleys are expected to see between 0.25-0.7 
inches of precipitation with this storm, with between 0.4 to 1.25 
inches in the mountains. Locally higher amounts are possible 
especially near Brian Head and in the upper Cottonwoods. Snow 
amounts are generally expected to be in the 4-8 inch range 
(especially above 8-9 kft) with higher amounts in the upper 
Cottonwoods and near Brian Head.

An upper ridge shifting into the area Saturday night through
Sunday will bring a period of drier and stable conditions. The
ridge will shift east for Monday, bringing increased southerly 
flow ahead of the next approaching storm system. This progressive
pattern will keep any strong inversions at bay.

The next storm looks to arrive over Utah late Monday night or 
Tuesday, impacting the area into Wednesday morning. Latest model 
trends suggest another quick-hitting progressive trough which will
bring another round of widespread precipitation to the area. 
However, this storm looks to be associated with a somewhat cooler 
airmass. LREF means of H7 temperatures for portions of northern 
Utah dip as low as -8C, which suggest snow levels down to at 
least 5 kft. 

As this trough exits the area, it will be followed quickly by yet
another storm system. While cluster analysis of global ensembles
show high confidence in a storm for the second half of next week,
there remain some differences regarding its timing and evolution.
This storm may arrive as early as Wednesday night but may hold off
until later Thursday. Additionally, some members are suggesting
that this will end up being another progressive trough while
others maintain a closed low solution which would bring an 
extended period of precipitation to the area. Latest cluster 
analysis shows an approximately 55%/45% split, favoring the closed
low solution slightly.

&&

.AVIATION...
KSLC...Decreasing CIGS are expected overnight as rain begins to 
overspread the airspace. Rain showers are expected to impact the 
terminal after 10z, with potential to create MVFR CIGS/VIS at 
times before showers become more spotty after 18z. In addition to 
CIG/VIS reductions, expect terrain obscuration throughout the day 
Saturday. Southerly winds prevail at the terminal until a cold 
front brings a switch to northwesterly winds after 18z.

REST OF UTAH AND SOUTHWEST WYOMING...Widespread rain showers will 
continue spreading northward overnight, resulting in decreasing CIGS 
across the entire region. While VFR conditions prevail overall for 
most terminals, there is a 30-50% chance for MVFR CIGS/VIS to 
develop at times under heavier rainfall. At higher elevation 
terminals such as KEVW, MVFR and potentially brief IFR conditions 
are likely as snow mixes in with rain. Winds remain southerly across 
the region overnight into Saturday morning, before a cold front 
pushes through the region, switching winds to prevailing northerly 
late Saturday morning into the early afternoon.

&&
